name: Fabry Disease

prevalence.estimate: 1 in 40,000 to 1 in 117,000 (classic); up to 1 in 3,000 including late-onset variants

ethnicAssociations: Higher late-onset variant frequency noted in Taiwanese and Italian newborn screening

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Expert consensus diagnostic criteria for Fabry disease

criteria.description: Deficient alpha-galactosidase A enzyme activity in plasma or leukocytes (males: <1% of normal; diagnostic)
Pathogenic variant identified in GLA gene
Characteristic clinical features (acroparesthesias, angiokeratomas, cornea verticillata, renal, cardiac, or cerebrovascular involvement)
Tissue biopsy showing globotriaosylceramide inclusions (lamellar bodies on electron microscopy)

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Males: deficient alpha-galactosidase A activity plus GLA mutation. Females: GLA mutation required (enzyme activity may be normal due to random X-inactivation); clinical features and elevated lyso-Gb3 are supportive.
diagnosticCriteria.notes: X-linked inheritance. Heterozygous females can be significantly affected. Late-onset cardiac and renal variants exist with residual enzyme activity and predominantly single-organ involvement. Newborn screening is available in some regions.

pathognomonic.notes: Whorl-like corneal deposits seen on slit-lamp; also seen with amiodarone use (drug history important)
Bathing trunk distribution (periumbilical, inguinal, buttocks, scrotum); develop in childhood-adolescence

common.symptomName: Acroparesthesias (burning pain in hands and feet)
common.notes: Often the earliest symptom in classic males; small fiber neuropathy. Triggered by heat, exercise, fever.

common.symptomName: Hypohidrosis or anhidrosis (reduced or absent sweating)
common.notes: Leads to heat intolerance and exercise intolerance

common.symptomName: Proteinuria progressing to chronic kidney disease
common.notes: Progressive; may lead to end-stage renal disease in 3rd-5th decade in classic males
May mimic hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; especially prominent in late-onset cardiac variant

occasional.notes: Both ischemic and hemorrhagic; mean age ~40 in males

occasional.symptomName: Cardiac arrhythmias (short PR, AV block, AF)

laboratory: Deficient alpha-galactosidase A enzyme activity in plasma or leukocytes (males)
Elevated plasma globotriaosylsphingosine (lyso-Gb3) - most sensitive biomarker
Note: enzyme activity may be normal in heterozygous females
imaging: Echocardiography showing concentric LVH (often mimics HCM)
Cardiac MRI with late gadolinium enhancement (posterolateral wall; T1 mapping shows low native T1 in early disease)
MRI brain showing white matter lesions and silent infarcts
Renal ultrasound showing increased cortical echogenicity
MRA showing dolichoectasia of vertebrobasilar system
genetic: Hemizygous males fully affected; heterozygous females variably affected
Late-onset mutations (e.g., N215S, IVS4+919G>A) cause predominantly cardiac variant
De novo mutations account for ~5% of cases
other: Renal biopsy showing zebra bodies (lamellar inclusions) on electron microscopy
Skin biopsy showing Gb3 deposits in vascular endothelium
Small fiber neuropathy on quantitative sensory testing or skin biopsy (intraepidermal nerve fiber density)
ECG showing short PR interval, LVH criteria

distinguishingFeatures: HCM typically has asymmetric septal hypertrophy (Fabry is concentric)
HCM has sarcomere gene mutations (MYH7, MYBPC3)
Low T1 mapping values on cardiac MRI suggest Fabry over HCM
Gaucher is autosomal recessive with glucocerebrosidase deficiency
Gaucher features hepatosplenomegaly and bone disease predominantly
Different storage material and enzyme deficiency
Acroparesthesias in children may be misdiagnosed as growing pains or rheumatic disease
Fabry has additional systemic features over time
Cardiac amyloidosis shows high T1 mapping (Fabry shows low T1)
Amyloidosis has elevated free light chains or TTR mutation
Different LGE pattern (subendocardial in amyloid vs posterolateral in Fabry)

redFlags: Young-onset stroke or TIA (<55 years) without traditional risk factors - screen for Fabry
Unexplained LVH especially with short PR interval - consider Fabry cardiac variant
Progressive proteinuria in young patient without diabetes or hypertension
Cryptogenic stroke with white matter lesions in young adult
Family history of renal failure, cardiomyopathy, or early stroke in X-linked pattern
references: Germain DP. Fabry disease. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2010;5:30.
Ortiz A, et al. Fabry disease revisited: Management and treatment recommendations for adult patients. Mol Genet Metab. 2018;123(4):416-427.
Mehta A, et al. Fabry disease: a review of current management strategies. QJM. 2010;103(9):641-59.

Desnick RJ, Brady R, Barranger J, et al. Fabry disease, an under-recognized multisystemic disorder: expert recommendations for diagnosis, management, and enzyme replacement therapy. Ann Intern Med. 2003;138(4):338-46.
